root.text.Part 1..11.0.revised_text: Qūm (קום) is an equivocal term, and one of its meanings[[fn:118]] is to stand upright, as opposed to being seated; e.g.: And he did not stand upright (ולא קם) nor stir before him (Esth. 5:9). It also contains the sense of stability and of confirmation or fulfillment; e.g.: May the Lord confirm (יקם) His word (I Sam. 1:23); And the field of Ephron was made sure (ויקם) (Gen. 23:17); The house in the walled city shall be confirmed (וקם) (Lev. 25:30); And the kingdom of Israel shall be established (וקמה) in your hand (I Sam. 24:21). It is always in this sense that the word קום is used of God; e.g.: Now will I arise (אקום), says the Lord (Ps. 12:6; Isa. 33:10), which means: now will I confirm My decree, My promise, and My threat; You will arise (תקום) and have mercy upon Zion (Ps. 102:14), that is to say, You will fulfill the promise of compassion which You made to it.
root.text.Part 1..11.0.rationale: Modernized academic terminology ('equivocal term' for homonym; 'was made sure' / 'be established' for biblical legal conveyances); standardized citations (Esth. 5:9, I Sam. 1:23, Gen. 23:17, Lev. 25:30, I Sam. 24:21, Ps. 12:6, Isa. 33:10; corrected Munk's citation error Ps. 114:14 to Ps. 102:14); updated Sion to Zion; preserved [[fn:118]].

root.text.Part 1..11.1.revised_text: And, as one who is resolved to do a thing is drawn toward action by standing upright, it is said of anyone who is stirred to an action that he stands upright; e.g.: For my son has stirred up (הקים, has caused to stand) my servant against me (I Sam. 22:8). This latter meaning also applies metaphorically to the execution of the decree of destruction pronounced by God against men who have deserved punishment; e.g.: And I will rise up (וקמתי) against the house of Jeroboam (Amos 7:9); And he shall rise up (וקם) against the house of evil-doers (Isa. 31:2). It may be that the words: "Now will I arise" (cited above) have this same meaning; likewise these words: "You will arise and have mercy upon Zion", that is to say, You will rise up against its enemies.
root.text.Part 1..11.1.rationale: Purged archaic/ungrammatical 'You shalt be upright' -> 'You will arise'; corrected miscited verse Isa. 21:2 to Isa. 31:2; standardized citations (I Sam. 22:8, Amos 7:9); Sion to Zion.

root.text.Part 1..11.2.revised_text: It is this sense that is expressed in many passages, and there can be no question there[[fn:119]] of standing upright or of being seated, which would be unworthy of the Divinity[[fn:120]]. "On high, say the Sages[[fn:121]], there is neither sitting (ישיבה) nor standing (עמידה)"; for ’amad (עמד) is used here in the sense of qām (קם).
root.text.Part 1..11.2.rationale: Rabbinic alignment: French 'docteurs' rendered as 'Sages' (Talmud Chagigah 15a); modernized prose; preserved [[fn:119]], [[fn:120]], [[fn:121]].

root.text.Part 1..12.0.revised_text: ’Amad (עמד) is an equivocal term which has (first) the meaning of standing upright, standing; e.g.: When he stood (בעמדו) before Pharaoh (Gen. 41:46); Though Moses and Samuel should stand (יעמד) before Me (Jer. 15:1); And he stood (עמד) by them (Gen. 18:8). It has (subsequently) the meaning of abstaining, ceasing (or stopping); e.g.: For they ceased (עמדו) and answered no more (Job 32:16); And she ceased (ותעמד) from bearing (Gen. 29:35). It has also the meaning of being stable, enduring (to be preserved, to subsist); e.g.: That they may endure (יעמדו) for many days (Jer. 32:14); You will be able to endure (עמוד) (Exod. 18:23); Its flavor remained (עמד) in it (Jer. 48:11), that is, it continued to subsist and be preserved; And His righteousness endures (עומדת) forever (Ps. 111:3), meaning it is stable and permanent. Whenever the verb עמד is applied to God, it is in this last sense; e.g.: And His feet shall stand (ועמדו), in that day, upon the Mount of Olives (Zech. 14:4), meaning His causes, that is, the events caused by Him, will endure and be confirmed. This will be further explained when we treat of the equivocal character of the word רגל (foot)[[fn:122]]. It is in this sense also that we must understand the words of God addressed to Moses[[fn:123]]: And as for you, stand (עמד) here by Me (Deut. 5:28 [Heb. v. 31]), and these words of Moses: I stood (אנכי עמד) between the Lord and you (ibid., 5:5)[[fn:124]].
root.text.Part 1..12.0.rationale: Repaired 13 missing opening <i> tags in v1 that caused severe tag imbalances; purged Latin OCR/drafting glosses ('ofstare', 'to ceasecessare', 'to endureconservare, subsistere'); standardized citations (Gen. 41:46, Jer. 15:1, Gen. 18:8, Job 32:16, Gen. 29:35, Jer. 32:14, Exod. 18:23, Jer. 48:11, Ps. 111:3, Zech. 14:4, Deut. 5:28, ibid., 5:5); preserved [[fn:122]], [[fn:123]], [[fn:124]].

root.text.Part 1..13.0.revised_text: As for the equivocal nature of the word Adam (אדם), it is primarily the proper name of the first man, a derived noun[[fn:125]] which, according to the text of Scripture, comes from adamāh (אדמה, earth)[[fn:126]]; next, it is the name of the species; e.g.: My spirit shall not always abide in man (באדם) (Gen. 6:3); Who knows if the spirit of the sons of men (בני האדם), etc. (Eccles. 3:21); The superiority of man (האדם) over the beast is nothing (ibid., 3:19). It is also a noun designating the multitude, that is to say, the common folk to the exclusion of men of distinction; e.g.: Both common men (בני אדם) and men of high degree (Ps. 49:3).
root.text.Part 1..13.0.rationale: Modernized academic prose ('equivocal nature', 'men of distinction'); standardized citations (Gen. 6:3, Eccles. 3:21, ibid., 3:19, Ps. 49:3); preserved [[fn:125]], [[fn:126]].

root.text.Part 1..13.1.revised_text: In this third sense it is also found in the following verses: And the sons of the Elohim[[fn:127]] saw the daughters of MEN (Gen. 6:2); Truly, you shall die like ORDINARY MEN (Ps. 82:7).
root.text.Part 1..13.1.rationale: Repaired drafting/OCR error: 'die like MAN vulgar' corrected to 'die like ORDINARY MEN' (French: 'mourrez comme L’HOMME vulgaire', Hebrew: 'אָכֵן כְּאָדָם תְּמוּתוּן'); standardized Gen. 6:2 and Ps. 82:7; preserved [[fn:127]].

root.text.Part 1..14.0.revised_text: Naṣav (נצב) or yaṣav (יצב). — Although these two roots are different, they have, as you know, the same meaning in all their conjugations.

root.text.Part 1..14.1.revised_text: It is an equivocal term which sometimes has the meaning of standing upright, rising; e.g.: And his sister stood (ותתצב) afar off (Exod. 2:4); The kings of the earth set themselves (יתיצבו) (Ps. 2:2); ... came out and stood (נצבים) (Num. 16:27); and sometimes that of being stable, permanent; e.g.: Your word stands firm (נצב) in the heavens (Ps. 119:89), meaning stable and permanent.
root.text.Part 1..14.1.rationale: Repaired punctuation and ellipsis; standardized citations (Exod. 2:4, Ps. 2:2, Num. 16:27, Ps. 119:89).

root.text.Part 1..14.2.revised_text: Every time this word is used in relation to the Creator, it has this latter meaning; e.g.: And behold, the Lord stood (נצב) above it (Gen. 28:13), being stable and permanent above it—that is to say, above the ladder whose one end is in heaven and the other on earth, and where all who ascend strive[[fn:128]] and mount upward, in order to perceive Him who is above of necessity[[fn:129]]; for He is stable and permanent at the summit of the ladder.
root.text.Part 1..14.2.rationale: Philosophical clarity (Munk note 2 on Arabic darūrah / Necessary Existent); standardized Gen. 28:13; preserved [[fn:128]], [[fn:129]].

root.text.Part 1..14.3.revised_text: It is clear, furthermore, that if I say here above it, it is with respect to the allegory that has been employed[[fn:130]]. The messengers of God are the prophets[[fn:131]], who are clearly called so in these passages: And He sent a messenger (Num. 20:16); And a messenger of the Lord went up from Gilgal to Bochim (Judg. 2:1). And how fittingly is it expressed in saying: they were ascending and descending—that is to say, by putting the verb to ascend before the verb to descend; for the prophet, after having ascended and attained certain rungs of the ladder, descends afterward with what he has learned in order to guide the inhabitants of the earth and instruct them, which is designated by the verb to descend, as we have explained[[fn:132]].
root.text.Part 1..14.3.rationale: Modernized prose ('rungs of the ladder' for degrees); standardized citations (Num. 20:16, Judg. 2:1); preserved [[fn:130]], [[fn:131]], [[fn:132]].

root.text.Part 1..14.4.revised_text: I return to our subject, namely that in the passage in question, נצב means stable, perpetual, permanent, and not standing upright like a physical body. In the same sense also must this passage be explained: And you shall stand (ונצבת) upon the rock (Exod. 33:21)[[fn:133]]; for you have already understood that naṣav (נצב) and ’amad (עמד) have the same meaning[[fn:134]] in this regard, and indeed God has said: Behold, I will stand (עומד) before you there upon the rock in Horeb (ibid., 17:6)[[fn:135]].
root.text.Part 1..14.4.rationale: Standardized citations (Exod. 33:21, ibid., 17:6); modernized syntax; preserved [[fn:133]], [[fn:134]], [[fn:135]].

root.text.Part 1..15.0.revised_text: Ṣūr (צור) is an equivocal term which primarily signifies rock[[fn:136]]; for example: You shall strike the rock (צור) (Exod. 17:6); then, in general, hard stone, like flint; for example: Knives of flint (צורים) (Josh. 5:2); finally, it is the name of the quarry from which stones are hewn; for example: Look to the rock (or quarry, צור) whence you were hewn (Isa. 51:1). In this last sense, the word has been used figuratively to designate the source and origin of all things; that is why the prophet, after having said: Look to the rock whence you were hewn, adds: Look to Abraham your father, etc. (ibid., v. 2), as though he were explaining: 'The rock whence you were hewn is Abraham your father; you must therefore follow in his footsteps, hold fast to his religion, and adopt his virtues; for the nature of the quarry must be reproduced in what has been extracted from it.'
root.text.Part 1..15.0.rationale: Clarified 'quarry' (Arabic ma'din / French mine); standardized citations (Exod. 17:6, Josh. 5:2, Isa. 51:1, ibid., v. 2); preserved [[fn:136]].

root.text.Part 1..15.1.revised_text: It is with respect to this last sense that God has been called צור (Rock); for He is the origin and efficient cause of everything outside of Himself. Thus it has been said: The Rock! (הצור) His work is perfect (Deut. 32:4); You were unmindful of the Rock that begot you (ibid., v. 18); Their Rock (צורם) had sold them (ibid., v. 30); And there is no rock like our God (I Sam. 2:2); An everlasting Rock (Isa. 26:4). Similarly, the words: And you shall stand upon the rock (Exod. 33:21) signify: 'Rely upon and hold fast to this reflection, that God is the origin of all things, for this is the portal by which you shall attain unto Him', as we have explained concerning the words[[fn:137]]: Behold, there is a place by Me (ibid.).
root.text.Part 1..15.1.rationale: Modernized academic phrasing; standardized citations (Deut. 32:4, ibid., v. 18, ibid., v. 30, I Sam. 2:2, Isa. 26:4, Exod. 33:21); preserved [[fn:137]].

root.text.Part 1..16.0.revised_text: One must not believe that it is with respect to metaphysical science alone that one was sparing[[fn:138]] toward the common people; for it was likewise so with the greater part of physical science[[fn:139]], and we have already cited on several occasions these words: 'Nor may the Ma‘aśeh Berēshīt be expounded before two persons'[[fn:140]]. This was observed not only among the adherents of divine Law[[fn:141]], but also among philosophers; and the ancient pagan sages expressed themselves on the principles of things in an obscure and enigmatic manner. Thus Plato and others before him called matter the female, and form the male[[fn:142]].
root.text.Part 1..16.0.rationale: Repaired drafting collision 'Thus,Plato et alii Plato and others before him' -> 'Thus Plato and others before him'; replaced archaic/pejorative 'niggardly' with 'sparing' (Arabic al-maḍnūn); refined 'adherents of divine Law' for ahl al-sharī'ah; preserved [[fn:138]], [[fn:139]], [[fn:140]], [[fn:141]], [[fn:142]].

root.text.Part 1..16.1.revised_text: [You know that the principles of beings that come into existence and perish are three in number: matter, form, and particular privation[[fn:143]], which is always conjoined with matter; for if matter were not accompanied by privation, it would not receive form, and in this manner privation is one of the principles. When the form arrives, this particular privation—I mean the privation of that arriving form—ceases, and another privation is joined to matter, and so on, as is explained in physics[[fn:144]].]
root.text.Part 1..16.1.rationale: Purged Latin drafting corruption 'three in number:materia, forma, et privatio matter, form, and particular privation particular'; modernized physics terminology ('come into existence and perish', 'receive form'); preserved [[fn:143]], [[fn:144]].

root.text.Part 1..16.2.revised_text: If, therefore, those who had nothing to lose by explaining themselves clearly made use in their teaching of figurative terms and employed allegories, with all the more reason must we, men of religious faith, avoid stating openly matters whose comprehension is difficult[[fn:145]] for the common people, or concerning which they might conceive the truth in a manner contrary to that which we intend[[fn:146]]. You must also impress this deeply upon your mind.
root.text.Part 1..16.2.rationale: Modernized academic prose ('whose comprehension is difficult', 'You must also impress this deeply upon your mind'); preserved [[fn:145]], [[fn:146]].

root.text.Part 1..17.0.revised_text: Qārav (קרב), nāga‘ (נגע), and nāgaš (נגש). — These three verbs sometimes have the meaning of approaching (or touching), of drawing near in space, and sometimes they express the conjunction of knowledge with the object known—a conjunction which is compared in a certain manner to one body drawing near to another body. — As for the primary meaning of qārav, which is that of drawing near in space, here are examples: When he came near (קרב) to the camp (Exod. 32:19); And Pharaoh drew near (הקריב) (ibid., 14:10). Nāga‘ primarily expresses the bringing into contact of one body with another; e.g.: And she touched (ותגע) his feet (ibid., 4:25); And he touched (ויגע) my mouth (Isa. 6:7). The primary meaning of nāgaš is to advance toward someone, to move toward him; e.g.: Then Judah came near (ויגש) unto him (Gen. 44:18).
root.text.Part 1..17.0.rationale: Corrected Hebrew OCR typo in Exod. 4:25: ותנע -> ותגע (nun to gimel); standardized citations (Exod. 32:19, ibid., 14:10, ibid., 4:25, Isa. 6:7, Gen. 44:18).

root.text.Part 1..17.1.revised_text: — The second meaning of these three words expresses a union through knowledge, an approach through perception, and not a spatial approach. Nāga‘ (נגע) has been employed in the sense of union through knowledge in the verse: For her judgment reaches (נגע) unto heaven[[fn:147]] (Jer. 51:9). In employing qārav (קרב), it has been said: And the cause that is too hard for you, you shall bring (תקריבון) unto me (Deut. 1:17), that is to say, you shall make it known to me; this verb has thus been used in the sense of making known that which is to be known. In employing nāgaš (נגש), it has been said: And Abraham drew near (ויגש), and said (Gen. 18:23); for he was then in a state of prophetic vision and trance, as will be explained[[fn:148]]. Elsewhere it is said: Inasmuch as this people draw near (נגש) with their mouth, and with their lips honor Me (Isa. 29:13).
root.text.Part 1..17.1.rationale: Standardized citations (Jer. 51:9, Deut. 1:17, Gen. 18:23, Isa. 29:13); modernized prose; preserved [[fn:147]], [[fn:148]].

root.text.Part 1..17.2.revised_text: Whenever one encounters in the prophetic books the expression qārav or nāgaš applying to a relationship between God and any creature whatsoever, it is always in this latter sense; for God is not a body, as will be demonstrated in this treatise, and consequently He, the Most High, approaches nothing and draws near to nothing, nor does anything draw near to Him or approach Him. For by excluding corporeality, one excludes space; and there can be no question of proximity, approach, distance, union, separation, contact, or succession.

root.text.Part 1..17.3.revised_text: I do not think you have any doubt in this regard, and there will be nothing obscure to you in these passages: The Lord is near to all who call upon Him (Ps. 145:18); They delight to draw near to God (Isa. 58:2); Drawing near to God is my good (Ps. 73:28); for in all these passages it is a question of drawing near through knowledge—that is to say, through intellectual perception, and not through spatial approach. It is the same in these passages: God so near to him (Deut. 4:7); Draw near and hear (ibid., 5:27); And Moses alone shall draw near to the Lord, but they shall not draw near (Exod. 24:2).
root.text.Part 1..17.3.rationale: Purged pseudo-biblical 'unto'; modernized prose; standardized citations (Ps. 145:18, Isa. 58:2, Ps. 73:28, Deut. 4:7, ibid., 5:27, Exod. 24:2).

root.text.Part 1..17.4.revised_text: However, if you wish to understand by the word ונגש, shall draw near, applied to Moses, that he could approach that place on the mountain where the light descended—that is to say, the glory of the Lord—you are at liberty to do so; only you must hold fast to this principle: whether an individual be at the center of the earth or at the summit of the ninth sphere[[fn:149]]—were that possible—he is not in the former case farther from God, nor in the latter nearer to Him; but one is near to God by perceiving Him, and whoever is ignorant of Him is far from Him. There is in this regard a great variety of gradations[[fn:150]] in drawing near and in withdrawing; and in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:151]] I shall explain what this relative superiority consists of in the perception of the Divinity.

root.text.Part 1..17.5.revised_text: — As for these words: Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke (Ps. 144:5), the meaning intended is: Cause Your decree to reach them—which, in turn, is to be understood metaphorically. Likewise the words: Touch his bone and his flesh (Job 2:5) signify: Cause Your affliction to descend upon him.
root.text.Part 1..17.5.rationale: CRITICAL REPAIR: Translated two biblical verses that were completely left in French in v1 ('Touche les montagnes, et qu’elles fument' -> 'Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke'; 'Et touche sa personne' -> 'Touch his bone and his flesh'); standardized Ps. 144:5 and Job 2:5.

root.text.Part 1..17.6.revised_text: Thus in each passage you must consider the verb נגע (to touch), as well as its derived forms, in conformity with the context as a whole: one expresses by this verb at times the contact of one body with another, and at times union through knowledge and the perception of something; for he who perceives a thing which he had not previously perceived draws near, as it were, to a thing that was distant from him. This must be well understood.

root.text.Part 1..18.0.revised_text: Mālē (מלא). — This is an equivocal term which the speakers of the Hebrew language employ in speaking of one body entering into another so as to fill it; e.g.: And she filled (ותמלא) her pitcher (Gen. 24:16); An omerful (מלא) (Exod. 16:32–33)[[fn:152]]; and this usage is frequent. It is also employed in the sense of the end and completion of a designated time; e.g.: And when her days were fulfilled (וימלאו) (Gen. 25:24); And when forty days were fulfilled for him (ibid., 50:3). It is then used to designate perfection and the highest degree of virtue; e.g.: And full (ומלא) with the blessing of the Lord (Deut. 33:23); He has filled them (מלא) with wisdom of heart (Exod. 35:35); And he was full (וימלא) of wisdom, understanding, and skill (I Kings 7:14).
root.text.Part 1..18.0.rationale: Major repair: Inverted <span dir="rtl"> tags in v1 moved from English words back to Hebrew terms; purged Latin drafting artifacts ('toimplere fill', 'offinis end andconsummatio consummation', 'denoteperfectio perfection'); standardized citations (Gen. 24:16, Exod. 16:32–33, Gen. 25:24, ibid., 50:3, Deut. 33:23, Exod. 35:35, I Kings 7:14); preserved [[fn:152]].

root.text.Part 1..18.1.revised_text: — It is in this sense that it was said: The whole earth is full of His glory (Isa. 6:3), which signifies: The whole earth bears witness to His perfection, that is to say, manifests Him everywhere. It is the same with the words: And the glory of the Lord filled (מלא) the tabernacle (Exod. 40:34). Every time you find the verb מלא, to fill, attributed to God, it is in this same sense, and it is by no means intended to say that there is a physical body filling a space. However, if you wish to admit that the glory of the Lord signifies the created light[[fn:153]], which everywhere is called glory, and that it was this light which filled the tabernacle, there is no harm in that.
root.text.Part 1..18.1.rationale: Standardized citations (Isa. 6:3, Exod. 40:34); polished academic prose; preserved [[fn:153]].

root.text.Part 1..19.0.revised_text: Rām (רם) is an equivocal term designating the elevation of place, as well as the elevation of rank—I mean majesty, nobility, and power. One reads, for example: And the ark was lifted up (ותרם) above the earth[[fn:154]] (Gen. 7:17), which belongs to the first sense; in the second sense, one reads, for example: I have exalted (הרימותי) one chosen out of the people (Ps. 89:20); Forasmuch as I exalted you (הרימותיך) out of the dust (I Kings 16:2)[[fn:155]]; Forasmuch as I exalted you (הרימותיך) from among the people (ibid., 14:7).
root.text.Part 1..19.0.rationale: Modernized academic style; standardized citations (Gen. 7:17, Ps. 89:20, I Kings 16:2, ibid., 14:7); preserved [[fn:154]], [[fn:155]].

root.text.Part 1..19.1.revised_text: Every time the verb rām (רם) is applied to God, it is taken in this second sense; for example: Be exalted (רומה) above the heavens, O God (Ps. 57:6).

root.text.Part 1..19.2.revised_text: In like manner, nāśā (נשׂא) conveys the sense of elevation of place and that of elevation of rank and increase in dignity[[fn:156]]. One reads, for example, in the first sense: And they loaded (וישׂאו) their grain upon their asses (Gen. 42:26); and there are many other passages where the verb נשׂא is taken in the sense of carrying and transporting, because a spatial elevation is involved. In the second sense one reads: And his kingdom shall be exalted (ותנשׂא) (Num. 24:7); And He bore them, and carried them (וינשׂאם) (Isa. 63:9); Why then do you exalt yourselves (תתנשׂאו) (Num. 16:3)?
root.text.Part 1..19.2.rationale: Modernized vocabulary; standardized citations (Gen. 42:26, Num. 24:7, Isa. 63:9, Num. 16:3); preserved [[fn:156]].

root.text.Part 1..19.3.revised_text: — In all instances where the verb nāśā (נשׂא) is applied to God, it is taken in this latter sense; for example: Lift up Yourself (הנשׂא), O judge of the earth! (Ps. 94:2); Thus says the High and Lofty One (ונשׂא) (Isa. 57:15)—where it is a matter of elevation, majesty[[fn:157]], and power, and not of spatial height.
root.text.Part 1..19.3.rationale: CRITICAL REPAIR: Translated two biblical verses left in French in v1 ('Élève-toi, ô juge de la terre' -> 'Lift up Yourself, O judge of the earth'; 'Ainsi a dit celui qui est haut et élevé' -> 'Thus says the High and Lofty One'); standardized Ps. 94:2 and Isa. 57:15; preserved [[fn:157]].

root.text.Part 1..19.4.revised_text: Perhaps you will find a difficulty in what I say: elevation of rank, majesty, and power; how, you will ask me, can you attach several ideas to one and the same meaning[[fn:158]]? But it will be explained to you further on that God, the Most High, for perfect men who comprehend His being, cannot be described by multiple attributes, and that all these numerous attributes indicating glorification, power, dominion, perfection, goodness, and the like, all revert to one single thing—and that thing is the divine essence, and not something external to that essence.
root.text.Part 1..19.4.rationale: Corrected archaic/ungrammatical 'canst you attach'; polished philosophical explanation; preserved [[fn:158]].

root.text.Part 1..19.5.revised_text: You will find further on chapters on the names and attributes of God; the purpose of the present chapter is solely to demonstrate that the words rām (רם) and nāśā (נשׂא), when applied to God, must be understood in the sense, not of a spatial elevation, but of an elevation of rank.
root.text.Part 1..19.5.rationale: Cleaned up quotation marks and transliterations ('ram' and 'nasa'); modernized prose.

root.text.Part 1..20.0.revised_text: ’Āvar (עבר) signifies primarily the same as the verb ’abara (عبر) in Arabic, and is predicated of a body that moves in space. It denotes first[[fn:159]] the movement of a living creature over a certain direct distance; e.g.: And he passed on (עבר) before them (Gen. 33:3); Pass on (עבֹר) before the people (Exod. 17:5); and this usage is frequent. Thenceforth it was employed figuratively to express the propagation of sounds through the air; e.g.: And they caused a proclamation to pass (ויעבירו קול) throughout the camp (Exod. 36:6); The report that I hear spreading (מעבירים) among the Lord's people (I Sam. 2:24).
root.text.Part 1..20.0.rationale: Corrected typo 'denots' -> 'denotes'; standardized citations (Gen. 33:3, Exod. 17:5, Exod. 36:6, I Sam. 2:24); preserved [[fn:159]].

root.text.Part 1..20.1.revised_text: It has been further employed to designate the manifestation of the light and the divine majesty which the prophets beheld in prophetic vision; e.g.: And behold, a smoking furnace, and a flaming torch that passed (עבר) between those pieces (Gen. 15:17), which took place in a prophetic vision, for it is said at the beginning of the account: A deep sleep fell upon Abram, etc. (ibid., v. 12). It is in accordance with this metaphor that we must understand the words: And I will pass (ועברתי) through the land of Egypt (Exod. 12:12), and every other similar passage.
root.text.Part 1..20.1.rationale: Modernized academic prose ('manifestation' for arrival); standardized citations (Gen. 15:17, ibid., v. 12, Exod. 12:12).

root.text.Part 1..20.2.revised_text: It is also used at times in speaking of one who, in performing an action, exceeds and goes beyond the proper limit; e.g.: And like a man whom wine has overcome (עברו)[[fn:160]] (Jer. 23:9).

root.text.Part 1..20.3.revised_text: Sometimes also it is employed in speaking of someone who passes[[fn:161]] beyond the mark which he had in view, and directs himself toward another goal and another terminus; e.g.: And he shot an arrow to make it pass beyond him (להעבירו) (I Sam. 20:36). It is in conformity with this figurative sense that one must, in my opinion, understand these words: And the Lord passed (ויעבר) before his face (Exod. 34:6), the pronoun in פניו, His face, referring to God. This is likewise what the Sages have maintained—namely, that פניו (His face) refers to God[[fn:162]]. Although they say this in the context of aggadot (or allegorical expositions) which would not be in place here, there is nevertheless in their statement something that corroborates our view. Thus, the pronoun in פניו referring to God, the explanation of the passage in question is, as it appears to me, as follows: Moses had requested a certain perception—namely, that which is designated by the expression seeing the face in the words: But My face shall not be seen (Exod. 33:23); and he was promised a perception inferior to that which he had requested—namely, that which is designated by the expression seeing the back in the words: And you shall see My back (ibid.). We have already called attention to this subject in the Mishneh Torah[[fn:163]]. The meaning intended here[[fn:164]] is therefore that God veiled from him that perception designated by the word פנים, face, and turned him toward another thing—I mean toward the knowledge of the actions attributed to God, which are taken for multiple attributes, as we shall explain[[fn:165]]. When I say: He veiled it from him, I mean thereby that this perception is veiled and inaccessible by its very nature; and that every perfect man who—his intellect having attained what is in its nature to perceive—then desires another, more profound perception[[fn:166]], finds his apprehension dulled or even destroyed[[fn:167]] [as will be explained in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:168]]], unless he is sustained by divine assistance, as God has said: And I will cover you with My hand while I pass by (Exod. 33:22).
root.text.Part 1..20.3.rationale: Rabbinic alignment: French 'docteurs' -> 'Sages'; aggadot transliterated cleanly; standardized citations (I Sam. 20:36, Exod. 34:6, Exod. 33:23, ibid., Mishneh Torah, Exod. 33:22); preserved all 8 footnotes [[fn:161]] through [[fn:168]].

root.text.Part 1..20.4.revised_text: As for the Chaldean Paraphrase, it has done here what it habitually does in such matters; for whenever it encounters anything attributed to God that is tainted with corporeality or partakes of corporeality, it posits the omission of the governing construct noun[[fn:169]], and ascribes the relation to something understood as being the construct annexed to the name of God[[fn:170]]. Thus, for example, the Targumist renders the words: And behold, the Lord stood above it (Gen. 28:13) by: "And behold, the glory of the Lord was stationed above it"; the words: The Lord watch between me and you (ibid., 31:49), he renders by: "May the Word of the Lord watch." Such is his constant procedure in his exposition; and he has done likewise with these words: And the Lord passed before his face, translating: "And the Lord caused His Majesty to pass before his face, and cried"; so that the entity which passed was, in his view, without doubt something created. The pronoun in פניו, his face, he refers to Moses, our master, so that the words על פניו (before his face) signify in his presence (or before him), as in that passage: And the present passed over before him (Gen. 32:22), which is likewise a sound and plausible interpretation. What confirms the explanation of Onkelos the proselyte are these words of Scripture: And it shall come to pass, while My glory passes by, etc. (Exod. 33:22), where it is clearly stated that what passes by is a created reality attributed to God, and not His essence [glorified be His name!]; and it is concerning this glory that He said: until I have passed by (ibid.); And the Lord passed before his face.
root.text.Part 1..20.4.rationale: Clarified grammatical construct noun (Arabic muḍāf / French annexe); modernized Targumic terminology (Onkelos / Targumist); standardized citations (Gen. 28:13, ibid., 31:49, Gen. 32:22, Exod. 33:22); preserved [[fn:169]], [[fn:170]].

root.text.Part 1..20.5.revised_text: But if it were absolutely necessary to assume an understood construct noun—as Onkelos constantly does, supplying as understood at times the glory, at times the Shekhinah or Majesty, and at times the divine Word, according to what suits each passage—we too might supply here, as the understood construct noun, the word קול, voice, so that the passage would virtually read: "And the voice of the Lord passed before him and cried." We have already explained above that the Hebrew language employs the verb עבר, to pass, in speaking of a voice; e.g.: They caused a voice to pass (that is, they proclaimed) throughout the camp. It would therefore be the voice that cried; and you should not find it improbable that crying is attributed to a voice, for Scripture employs precisely the same expression in speaking of the speech of God addressed to Moses; e.g.: And he heard the voice speaking unto him (Num. 7:89); just as the verb דבר, to speak, was attributed to the voice, so here the verb קרא, to cry, to call, was attributed to the voice. Something similar is found expressly in Scripture—I mean that Scripture explicitly attributes to the voice the verbs אמר, to say, and קרא, to cry; e.g.: A VOICE SAYS: Cry! And one answered: What shall I cry? (Isa. 40:6). — It would therefore be necessary, according to this ellipsis, to explain the passage in question thus: "And a voice from God passed before him and cried: The Lord, the Lord! etc."; the repetition of the name the Lord serving as a vocative—God being the One addressed in the call—just as elsewhere we find: Moses, Moses! or Abraham, Abraham! — This likewise is a very excellent interpretation.
root.text.Part 1..20.5.rationale: Clarified linguistic and Targumic construct usage; standardized citations (Num. 7:89, Isa. 40:6); modernized syntax.

root.text.Part 1..20.6.revised_text: You will not find it strange that a subject so profound and so difficult of apprehension should be susceptible of so many diverse interpretations, for this presents no obstacle to our present purpose. You are therefore free to choose whichever opinion you will: you may admit either that this entire awe-inspiring scene was indubitably a prophetic vision, and that all the efforts of Moses[[fn:171]] tended toward intellectual perceptions, so that what he sought, what was denied him, and what he perceived were all alike intellectual, without the intervention of any sense-perception, as we interpreted it at the beginning; or else, that there was simultaneously a perception by means of the sense of sight, but which had for its object a created thing, through the contemplation of which the perfection of intellectual perception was attained, as Onkelos interpreted—provided that this perception by means of sight was not itself a prophetic vision[[fn:172]], like that which is recounted of Abraham: And behold, a smoking furnace, and a burning torch that passed, etc.; or finally, that there was also therewith a perception by means of the sense of hearing, and that what passed before him was the voice, which undoubtedly was also something created. Choose, therefore, whichever opinion you please; for my sole aim is that you should not believe that the verb ויעבר, He passed, has here the same sense as עבֹר in the passage: Pass on before the people (Exod. 17:5). For God [blessed be He!] is not a body, and movement cannot be attributed to Him; it cannot therefore be said that He passed (עבר), according to the primary signification of that word in the language.
root.text.Part 1..20.6.rationale: Purged archaic 'unto' ('movement cannot be attributed to Him'); modernized prose; standardized citations (Gen. 15:17, Exod. 17:5); preserved [[fn:171]], [[fn:172]].
